In autumn and winter, respiration and decomposition dominate and the concentration rises, producing the annual sawtooth visible in long-term atmospheric records.

Skeletal muscle is organised into a precise hierarchy. Each muscle is a bundle of fibres, each fibre a single multinucleate cell packed with myofibrils, and each myofibril a chain of sarcomeres. The sarcomere is the contractile unit, its repeating arrangement of overlapping thick myosin and thin actin filaments producing the striated appearance of the tissue under the microscope.

Excitation-contraction coupling links the electrical signal of an action potential to the mechanical event of contraction. The action potential travels down the transverse tubules to voltage sensors that are physically coupled to calcium-release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Their opening floods the cytosol with calcium, which binds troponin and permits the actin-myosin interaction that generates force.

Skeletal muscle contains a mix of fibre types suited to different demands. Slow oxidative fibres are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, resist fatigue, and sustain posture and endurance activity. Fast glycolytic fibres contract rapidly and powerfully but tire quickly, relying on anaerobic metabolism. The proportion of each type, partly heritable and partly trainable, shapes an individual's athletic aptitude.

The force a muscle can produce depends on the degree of overlap between thick and thin filaments, summarised by the length-tension relationship. At an optimal sarcomere length the maximum number of cross-bridges can form. If the muscle is stretched too far the filaments barely overlap, and if it is too short the thin filaments collide, and in both cases the force the sarcomere can generate declines.

A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates. Fine movements such as those of the eye are controlled by small motor units of a few fibres each, while powerful muscles of the leg have units of many hundreds. The nervous system grades muscle force by recruiting more units and by increasing their firing rate.

Smooth muscle lines hollow organs and the walls of blood vessels and contracts more slowly than skeletal muscle. It lacks sarcomeres and troponin, and calcium instead activates contraction by binding calmodulin, which switches on myosin light-chain kinase. The kinase phosphorylates myosin to enable cross-bridge cycling, and the slow dephosphorylation by a phosphatase allows smooth muscle to maintain tone with little energy expenditure.

Working muscle draws on several energy systems with different time courses. A small reservoir of stored ATP and phosphocreatine powers the first few seconds of intense effort. Anaerobic glycolysis then supplies energy for activity lasting up to a couple of minutes, and aerobic oxidation of carbohydrate and fat sustains prolonged exercise, becoming the dominant source as duration increases.

Muscle adapts to the demands placed upon it. Resistance training drives hypertrophy, increasing fibre cross-sectional area by adding myofibrils, while endurance training increases mitochondrial density and capillary supply without much change in size. Disuse has the opposite effect, with immobilised or unloaded muscle losing protein and shrinking, an atrophy that the nervous and endocrine systems together regulate.

Skeletal muscle retains a capacity for regeneration thanks to satellite cells, quiescent stem cells lodged between the fibre membrane and the basal lamina. Injury activates them to proliferate; some daughters fuse to existing fibres or form new ones, repairing the damage, while others self-renew to replenish the satellite pool. Their gradual decline with age contributes to the muscle loss of senescence.

The giant protein titin spans half the sarcomere, running from the Z-disc to the central M-line. It acts as a molecular spring, its extensible segments unfolding and refolding to generate the passive elastic force that resists overstretch and helps the relaxed sarcomere recoil to its resting length. Titin also serves as a template that organises the orderly assembly of the sarcomere.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network that returns interstitial fluid to the bloodstream. Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries take up the fluid filtered from blood capillaries along with proteins and immune cells. One-way valves and the squeezing of surrounding muscles propel the lymph through a series of lymph nodes and finally into large veins near the heart.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: The innate immune system provides an immediate, non-specific first line of defence. Physical barriers such as skin and mucous membranes exclude most microbes, while antimicrobial peptides, lysozyme, and the acidic pH of the stomach destroy those that breach the surface. Unlike adaptive immunity, the innate response is fully present from birth and does not improve on repeated exposure to the same pathogen.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Phagocytes recognise pathogens through pattern recognition receptors that bind conserved microbial molecules. Toll-like receptors detect features such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, and viral nucleic acids. Engagement of these receptors triggers signalling that activates the phagocyte, induces inflammatory gene expression, and links the rapid innate response to the slower mobilisation of adaptive immunity.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Inflammation is the coordinated tissue response to infection or injury. Resident cells release mediators such as histamine and prostaglandins that dilate local blood vessels and raise their permeability. The increased blood flow and leakage of plasma produce the redness, heat, and swelling of inflammation, while chemotactic signals recruit neutrophils from the circulation to the site within hours.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Natural killer cells patrol the body for stressed and abnormal cells without prior sensitisation. They monitor the level of MHC class I on cell surfaces, sparing healthy cells that display it normally. Many viruses and tumours downregulate MHC class I to evade T cells, but this loss of the inhibitory signal exposes them to natural killer cells, which deliver a lethal hit of perforin and granzymes.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Lymph nodes are organised filtering stations positioned along the lymphatic vessels. Lymph percolates through a meshwork in which macrophages trap particulate antigen, while dendritic cells arriving from the tissues present antigen to lymphocytes. The architecture brings rare antigen-specific lymphocytes into contact with their antigen, making the lymph node the principal site where adaptive immune responses are initiated.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and the first responders to bacterial infection. They engulf microbes into phagosomes and kill them with reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial granule contents. Some neutrophils undergo a distinct death in which they extrude a web of DNA studded with antimicrobial proteins, an extracellular trap that ensnares and kills microbes outside the cell.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: The spleen filters the blood much as lymph nodes filter lymph. Its red pulp removes aged and damaged erythrocytes from the circulation, and macrophages there recycle their iron. The white pulp is lymphoid tissue that mounts immune responses against blood-borne pathogens, which is why people without a spleen are especially vulnerable to infection by encapsulated bacteria.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: Interferons are signalling proteins that orchestrate antiviral defence. A virus-infected cell secretes type I interferons, which bind receptors on neighbouring cells and induce hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes. The products of those genes degrade viral RNA, block translation, and otherwise establish an antiviral state, so that the infection is contained even before adaptive immunity engages.

subtopic: the lymphatic system and innate immunity
sentence: The innate immune system shows a form of immunological memory once thought unique to adaptive immunity. After certain infections or vaccinations, monocytes and natural killer cells undergo lasting metabolic and epigenetic changes that leave them primed to respond more vigorously to a later, unrelated challenge. This phenomenon, termed trained immunity, broadens the classical division between innate and adaptive defence.

Most fungi grow as a network of thread-like filaments called hyphae, which together form a mycelium. Each hypha extends only at its tip, where vesicles delivered along the cytoskeleton supply new cell wall and membrane. The mycelium explores the substrate, secreting digestive enzymes externally and absorbing the liberated nutrients, a mode of nutrition that makes fungi the principal decomposers of woody plant material.

The fungal cell wall is built largely of chitin and glucans rather than the cellulose of plants. Chitin, a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine, forms microfibrils that give the wall tensile strength, while branched glucans cross-link the structure. Because these polymers and their synthetic enzymes have no counterpart in human cells, they are favoured targets for antifungal drugs.

Lichens are composite organisms formed from a fungus and one or more photosynthetic partners, either algae or cyanobacteria. The fungal partner provides structure, anchorage, and protection from desiccation, while the photosynthetic partner supplies fixed carbon. The partnership lets lichens colonise bare rock and other harsh surfaces where neither organism could survive alone, often as pioneer species.

Many fungi reproduce by both sexual and asexual means. Asexual spores are produced rapidly and in vast numbers, dispersing the genotype without recombination. Sexual reproduction in fungi often involves a prolonged stage in which two genetically distinct nuclei coexist in the same cytoplasm without fusing, the dikaryon, which fuses only shortly before meiosis produces the sexual spores.

Yeasts are unicellular fungi that typically multiply by budding, with a small daughter cell pinching off from the mother. The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has long served as a model eukaryote because it is easy to culture, has a compact genome, and undergoes the same fundamental processes of cell division, secretion, and gene regulation as the cells of multicellular organisms.

Some fungi manipulate the behaviour of their hosts. The fungus Ophiocordyceps infects carpenter ants and, as it grows, drives the ant to climb vegetation and clamp its jaws onto a leaf vein before dying. The fungus then erupts a fruiting structure from the ant's head, releasing spores from an elevated position that maximises their dispersal onto the foraging trails below.

Fungal spores are dispersed by mechanisms tuned to their habitat. Many mushrooms discharge spores using a surface-tension catapult, in which a water droplet condenses on the spore and its sudden coalescence flings the spore off the gill. Other fungi rely on wind, water, or animal vectors, and some build pressurised structures that shoot spore masses several metres into the air.

Mycorrhizal fungi form intimate associations with the roots of most land plants. The fungus extends a vast hyphal network through the soil, scavenging phosphorus and other nutrients beyond the reach of root hairs, and delivers them to the plant in exchange for photosynthetic sugars. This partnership is ancient, and fossil evidence suggests it helped the first plants colonise land.

Fungi defend their resources and attack other organisms with an arsenal of secondary metabolites. Penicillium moulds secrete penicillin, which kills competing bacteria, and many fungi produce toxins that deter animals or poison hosts. The same biosynthetic capacity yields compounds of medical value, including the immunosuppressant cyclosporine and the cholesterol-lowering statins.

Pathogenic fungi cause devastating diseases of plants and animals. The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis infects amphibian skin, disrupting its role in water and electrolyte balance, and has driven population declines and extinctions worldwide. Fungal diseases of crops, such as the wheat rusts, threaten food security and have repeatedly forced the breeding of resistant cultivars.

Transcription factors control which genes a cell expresses by binding short, specific DNA sequences in promoters and enhancers. A typical factor has a DNA-binding domain that recognises its target sequence and a separate activation or repression domain that contacts the transcriptional machinery. Combinations of factors bound at a single regulatory region integrate multiple signals to set the rate of transcription.

The lac operon of Escherichia coli is a classic example of inducible gene regulation. In the absence of lactose, a repressor protein binds the operator and blocks transcription of the genes for lactose metabolism. When lactose is present, a metabolite of it binds the repressor, changing its shape so it releases the operator and allows transcription to proceed.

Enhancers are regulatory DNA elements that can boost transcription of a gene from a great distance, even tens of kilobases away and regardless of orientation. They function by binding activator proteins and then looping through space to contact the gene's promoter. The looping is constrained within topological domains, so an enhancer normally acts only on genes within its own domain.

Cell identity is established by combinations of master regulatory transcription factors. A small set of such factors can be sufficient to specify a cell type, and forced expression of the right combination can convert one differentiated cell into another. The conversion of fibroblasts into muscle cells by the single factor MyoD was an early demonstration of this principle.

Transcription is regulated not only by activators and repressors but by the general accessibility of the chromatin. Nucleosomes positioned over a promoter can occlude the sites where transcription factors must bind. ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling complexes slide or evict these nucleosomes, and their recruitment by sequence-specific factors is often the decisive step in switching a gene on.

Signal-activated transcription factors translate extracellular cues into changes in gene expression. The factor NF-kappaB is held inactive in the cytoplasm by an inhibitor; an inflammatory signal triggers degradation of the inhibitor, freeing NF-kappaB to enter the nucleus and switch on immune-response genes. The pathway converts a transient surface signal into a programme of new transcription.

Gene regulatory networks built from transcription factors generate the dynamic behaviour of cells. A factor that represses its own gene forms a negative feedback loop that stabilises expression, while two factors that mutually repress each other form a switch with two stable states. Such circuit motifs, recurring across organisms, underlie cellular memory and the irreversible decisions of differentiation.

Transcription factors recognise their DNA targets through structured binding domains. The zinc finger uses a zinc ion to stabilise a compact fold whose surface reads three base pairs, and fingers strung together read longer sequences. The helix-turn-helix and the leucine zipper are other recurring motifs, each presenting an alpha helix that inserts into the major groove of the double helix.

Eukaryotic transcription factors rarely act alone; they recruit large coactivator and corepressor complexes that carry the catalytic activities needed to change a gene's output. Coactivators include enzymes that acetylate histones to open chromatin, while corepressors include histone deacetylases that compact it. The factor thus serves as an address label, and the recruited complex does the work.

Cells use combinatorial control to generate many expression patterns from a limited set of transcription factors. A gene's regulatory region carries binding sites for several factors, and the gene is expressed only where the right combination of factors is present at adequate levels. This logic lets a few hundred factors specify the thousands of distinct expression states found across the cell types of an animal.

MicroRNAs are short RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression after transcription. A microRNA is processed from a longer precursor and loaded into a silencing complex, which it guides to messenger RNAs bearing a complementary sequence, usually in the untranslated region. Binding represses translation and promotes degradation of the target, and a single microRNA can dampen the output of hundreds of genes.

RNA interference is a defence and regulatory pathway triggered by double-stranded RNA. The enzyme Dicer cleaves long double-stranded RNA into short interfering RNAs, one strand of which is loaded into the Argonaute protein. The loaded complex then finds and cleaves messenger RNAs of matching sequence, a mechanism that protects cells against viruses and transposons and is widely exploited as a laboratory tool.

Long noncoding RNAs are transcripts longer than two hundred nucleotides that are not translated into protein. The lncRNA Xist coats one of the two X chromosomes in female mammalian cells and recruits silencing complexes that compact the chromosome into transcriptionally inert heterochromatin. This X-chromosome inactivation equalises the dosage of X-linked genes between the sexes.

Ribosomal RNA is not merely structural scaffolding for the ribosome; it is the catalyst. The peptidyl transferase reaction that joins amino acids into a chain is carried out by the large subunit ribosomal RNA, with no protein side chains positioned to perform the chemistry. The ribosome is therefore a ribozyme, evidence that RNA-based catalysis preceded the dominance of protein enzymes.

Transfer RNA is the adaptor that links the genetic code to protein synthesis. Each tRNA carries an anticodon that pairs with a messenger RNA codon at one end and the corresponding amino acid at the other. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases enforce the code by attaching the correct amino acid to each tRNA, an act of molecular recognition on which the fidelity of translation depends.

Riboswitches are regulatory segments within messenger RNAs that bind small metabolites directly, without any protein intermediary. When the target metabolite is abundant it binds the riboswitch and changes its folded structure, which in turn alters transcription termination or the accessibility of the ribosome binding site. The mechanism lets a gene sense the concentration of its own end product.

Small nucleolar RNAs guide the chemical modification of other RNAs. Each snoRNA base-pairs with a specific site on a ribosomal RNA or small nuclear RNA and positions an associated enzyme to install a modification, typically a methyl group or a conversion of uridine to pseudouridine. These modifications cluster in functionally important regions and fine-tune the activity of the modified RNA.

The piwi-interacting RNA pathway protects the germline genome from transposable elements. These small RNAs, distinct from microRNAs, are produced from clusters of transposon-derived sequence and loaded into Piwi proteins. The complex silences active transposons both by cleaving their transcripts and by directing repressive chromatin marks to their genomic copies, safeguarding the integrity of the inherited genome.

Some RNA molecules act as enzymes in their own right. The self-splicing group I introns excise themselves from a precursor RNA without protein assistance, and the small hammerhead ribozyme found in certain plant viroids cleaves its own backbone at a defined site. Such catalytic RNAs support the hypothesis of an early RNA world in which RNA both stored information and catalysed reactions.

Enhancer RNAs are transcribed from active enhancer elements and were once dismissed as transcriptional noise. Evidence now indicates that the act of transcribing them, and the RNAs themselves, can stabilise the contact between an enhancer and its target promoter. Their abundance correlates closely with the activity of the genes the enhancers regulate, making them useful markers of functional enhancers.

Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences that cap the ends of linear chromosomes and protect them from being recognised as broken DNA. Because the replication machinery cannot fully copy the very end of a strand, telomeres shorten with each cell division. When they become critically short, the cell interprets the loss as damage and enters senescence, placing a limit on the number of times it can divide.

The enzyme telomerase counteracts telomere shortening by extending the chromosome ends with new repeats. It carries its own RNA template and adds DNA to the telomere, a reverse-transcription reaction. Telomerase is active in germ cells and stem cells but largely silent in ordinary somatic cells, and its reactivation is a common step in the path to cancer.

Mitochondria accumulate damage over a lifetime, and their decline is a recurring theme in theories of ageing. Reactive oxygen species generated as a by-product of respiration can damage mitochondrial DNA, proteins, and lipids. Impaired mitochondria produce less ATP and may leak more reactive species, and the gradual loss of mitochondrial quality contributes to the functional decline of energy-demanding tissues.

Caloric restriction extends lifespan in organisms ranging from yeast to mice. Reducing food intake without malnutrition slows the rate of ageing and delays age-related disease, an effect linked to nutrient-sensing pathways. The kinase target of rapamycin and the sirtuin family of enzymes both respond to nutrient status and influence how long an organism lives, making them targets for interventions on ageing.

Senescent cells accumulate in ageing tissues and contribute actively to their decline. Although they no longer divide, these cells remain metabolically active and secrete a mixture of inflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and proteases known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. This secretion disrupts the surrounding tissue, and experimentally clearing senescent cells from aged mice improves their healthspan.

Patterns of DNA methylation change in a remarkably predictable way with age. By measuring methylation at a few hundred selected sites in the genome, an epigenetic clock can estimate an individual's age to within a few years. When the methylation-predicted age exceeds chronological age, the discrepancy is associated with elevated risk of disease and mortality, suggesting the clock tracks biological rather than calendar time.

Proteostasis, the maintenance of a healthy protein population, declines with age. The capacity of chaperones to refold damaged proteins and of the proteasome and autophagy to clear them both diminish, allowing misfolded and aggregated proteins to accumulate. This failure of protein quality control underlies the late onset of many neurodegenerative diseases and is considered a hallmark of ageing.

Stem cell function declines with age, reducing the capacity of tissues to repair and renew themselves. Aged haematopoietic stem cells become biased toward producing myeloid cells, and aged muscle satellite cells respond less vigorously to injury. The decline reflects both intrinsic changes in the stem cells and a deterioration of the niche that normally instructs them.

Ageing rates vary enormously across species in ways that challenge simple wear-and-tear explanations. Some bats and birds live many times longer than ground-dwelling mammals of similar size, and the naked mole-rat resists cancer and shows little increase in mortality with age. These exceptional species are studied for the cellular adaptations that decouple their lifespans from body size and metabolic rate.

The evolutionary theory of ageing explains senescence as a consequence of declining selection with age. Because few individuals survive to old age in the wild, mutations that harm only the elderly are weakly opposed by selection and accumulate. Genes that benefit early reproduction at a later cost can even be favoured, a trade-off called antagonistic pleiotropy that links the force of selection to the evolution of lifespan.

Amphibian skin is thin, moist, and highly permeable, serving as a major organ of gas exchange. Many salamanders of the family Plethodontidae have no lungs at all and respire entirely across the skin and the lining of the mouth. The same permeability that permits cutaneous respiration leaves amphibians vulnerable to water loss and to absorbing pollutants directly from their environment.

Most amphibians undergo metamorphosis, a hormonally driven transformation from an aquatic larva to a terrestrial adult. A surge of thyroid hormone triggers the remodelling, in which a tadpole resorbs its tail and gills, grows limbs, and reorganises its gut and nervous system. The same hormone orchestrates the destruction of larval tissues and the construction of adult ones in a precisely timed programme.

In many reptiles, the sex of an embryo is determined not by chromosomes but by the temperature at which the egg is incubated. In crocodiles and many turtles, eggs held at certain temperatures during a sensitive window develop as one sex and at other temperatures as the other. The mechanism makes these animals sensitive to climate, since shifting temperatures can skew the sex ratio of hatchlings.

Snake venoms are complex cocktails of proteins and peptides delivered through specialised fangs. Some venoms are dominated by neurotoxins that block transmission at the neuromuscular junction, causing paralysis, while others are rich in enzymes that destroy tissue and disrupt blood clotting. The venom serves both to subdue prey and to begin its digestion before it is swallowed whole.

The amniotic egg was a key innovation that freed reptiles from dependence on water for reproduction. Extraembryonic membranes enclose the embryo: the amnion holds it in a private pool of fluid, the chorion and allantois handle gas exchange and waste storage, and the yolk sac supplies nutrients. The shelled, self-contained egg could be laid on dry land, opening terrestrial habitats to vertebrate reproduction.

Many lizards can shed their tails to escape a predator, a defence called caudal autotomy. Fracture planes built into the tail vertebrae allow it to break cleanly, and the detached tail thrashes vigorously, distracting the predator while the lizard flees. The lizard can regenerate a replacement, though the new tail is supported by a rod of cartilage rather than the original segmented bone.

Some frogs survive being frozen solid through the winter. As ice forms in their body cavities, they flood their cells with glucose and other cryoprotectants that lower the freezing point inside the cells and limit dehydration. The heart stops and the frog appears dead, yet when spring thaws the tissues the protected cells resume function and the animal revives.

Reptiles regulate their body temperature by behaviour rather than metabolism, a strategy called ectothermy. A lizard shuttles between sun and shade, presses its body against warm rock, or changes its posture and skin colour to control how much heat it absorbs. This behavioural thermoregulation lets reptiles maintain a fairly stable working temperature while spending far less energy than an endothermic mammal.

Chameleons project their tongues at prey with extraordinary speed, the tongue accelerating off the mouth in a few hundredths of a second. The mechanism is a catapult: muscles slowly load elastic tissue around a cartilage in the tongue, and a trigger releases the stored energy all at once. Because elastic recoil is not limited by muscle contraction speed, the strike is faster than muscle alone could achieve.

The poison of dart frogs is not made by the frogs themselves but acquired from their diet of ants, mites, and other small arthropods. Captive-raised frogs fed on innocuous insects never become toxic. The frogs sequester the dietary alkaloids in skin glands, and their bright warning colouration advertises the chemical defence to potential predators that have learned to avoid them.

Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth mechanically break food apart and saliva moistens it and begins chemical breakdown. Salivary amylase starts hydrolysing starch into shorter sugars, and lingual lipase makes a small contribution to fat digestion. The chewed and lubricated bolus is then swallowed and propelled toward the stomach by waves of muscular contraction in the oesophagus.

The stomach is a muscular reservoir that both stores and processes food. Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid that denatures proteins and kills many ingested microbes, while chief cells release pepsinogen that the acid converts to the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin. A layer of mucus and bicarbonate secreted by surface cells shields the stomach lining from being digested by its own acid.

Most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption occur in the small intestine. Pancreatic enzymes delivered into its lumen break down carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and nucleic acids, while bile from the liver emulsifies fat into fine droplets. The lining is folded into villi and microvilli that multiply the absorptive surface enormously, and nutrients pass through the epithelium into blood and lymph.

The liver occupies a central place in digestion and metabolism. Blood draining the intestine flows first to the liver through the hepatic portal vein, so absorbed nutrients pass through it before reaching the rest of the body. The liver buffers blood glucose, synthesises plasma proteins, detoxifies many compounds, and produces bile, which it secretes for the digestion and absorption of dietary fat.

The large intestine receives the residue that the small intestine has not absorbed. It recovers water and electrolytes, compacting the contents into faeces, and it harbours a dense community of bacteria that ferment undigested fibre. The fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that the colonic lining absorbs and uses as fuel, and it also produces vitamins such as vitamin K.

Movement through the digestive tract is driven by peristalsis, a coordinated wave of muscular contraction. Circular muscle contracts behind the bolus and relaxes ahead of it, squeezing the contents forward. This reflex is organised by the enteric nervous system, an extensive network of neurons embedded in the gut wall that can coordinate digestion with little input from the brain.

Ruminant mammals such as cattle digest plant fibre with the help of a specialised four-chambered stomach. The largest chamber, the rumen, is a fermentation vat where microbes break cellulose into absorbable fatty acids. The animal regurgitates and rechews the partially digested material, and the microbial biomass itself is later digested, supplying the ruminant with much of its protein.

Digestion is coordinated by hormones released from the gut wall in response to food. The arrival of acidic chyme in the small intestine triggers secretin, which prompts the pancreas to release bicarbonate. Fatty and protein-rich food triggers cholecystokinin, which stimulates the release of pancreatic enzymes and bile and slows gastric emptying, matching the supply of digestive secretions to the meal.

The absorptive cells of the small intestine carry specific transporters for each class of nutrient. Glucose and amino acids are taken up by sodium-coupled cotransporters, while the products of fat digestion diffuse into the cell and are reassembled into triglycerides. These are packaged with proteins into chylomicrons, which enter the lymphatic vessels rather than the blood capillaries.

Carnivores, herbivores, and omnivores have digestive tracts shaped by their diets. Herbivores possess long intestines and enlarged fermentation chambers to extract energy from tough plant material, whereas carnivores have short, simple guts suited to easily digested flesh. The length of the gut relative to body size therefore reflects the difficulty of digesting an animal's characteristic food.

The vertebrate eye forms an image by refracting light onto the retina. The cornea provides most of the fixed refractive power, while the lens adjusts focus through accommodation. In mammals, ciliary muscles change the shape of the elastic lens to focus on near or distant objects, and a failure of this system to project the image precisely on the retina produces the common refractive errors of vision.

The retina contains two classes of photoreceptor with complementary roles. Rods are extremely sensitive and support vision in dim light but do not distinguish colour, while cones operate in bright light and provide colour vision and fine detail. Cones are concentrated in the fovea, a small central pit where visual acuity is highest, and rods dominate the peripheral retina.

Signals generated in the photoreceptors are processed within the retina before they ever leave the eye. Bipolar cells relay the signal toward the ganglion cells, while horizontal and amacrine cells mediate lateral interactions that sharpen contrast and detect motion. The retina is thus a piece of the brain, performing substantial computation on the visual scene at its first stage.

Ganglion cells have receptive fields organised in a centre-surround pattern. A cell may be excited by light falling on the centre of its field and inhibited by light on the surround, or the reverse. This arrangement makes the cell respond strongly to edges and changes in illumination while ignoring uniform brightness, an efficient first encoding of the structure in a visual scene.

The eye adapts over a wide range of light intensities. In bright light the pupil constricts and cone-based vision dominates, while in darkness the pupil dilates and the much more sensitive rod system takes over. Full dark adaptation depends on the slow regeneration of the rod pigment rhodopsin, which can take half an hour to reach maximum sensitivity.

Compound eyes, found in insects and crustaceans, are built from many independent units called ommatidia, each with its own lens and small cluster of photoreceptors. Each ommatidium samples a narrow cone of the visual field, and the brain assembles the array of samples into an image. The design gives a wide field of view and excellent motion detection at the cost of fine spatial resolution.

Visual information leaves the eye along the optic nerve and is partly crossed at the optic chiasm, so that each side of the brain receives input from the opposite half of the visual field. After a relay in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, the signals reach the primary visual cortex, where the first cortical analysis of the scene begins.

Eyes have evolved independently many times across the animal kingdom, ranging from simple pigment cups that sense only the direction of light to image-forming camera and compound eyes. Despite this independent origin, a shared set of regulatory genes, including the master gene Pax6, directs eye development in animals as different as flies and mammals, evidence of a deeply conserved genetic toolkit.

The retinal pigment epithelium is a layer of cells behind the photoreceptors that is essential to their function. It absorbs stray light, supplies the photoreceptors with nutrients, recycles the spent visual pigment back into a usable form, and engulfs the worn-out tips that the photoreceptors continually shed. Failure of this support layer leads to degeneration of the photoreceptors and loss of vision.

Some animals see wavelengths invisible to humans. Many birds and insects have a photoreceptor sensitive to ultraviolet light, revealing patterns on flowers and plumage that humans cannot perceive. The mantis shrimp carries an exceptional set of a dozen or more photoreceptor classes, suggesting its visual system encodes colour in a way fundamentally unlike the comparison-based scheme of vertebrates.

Walking and running are distinguished by the way the body exchanges energy with each stride. In a walk the body vaults over a relatively stiff supporting leg, trading kinetic energy for gravitational potential energy like an inverted pendulum. In a run the leg behaves as a spring, storing energy in tendons during the first half of contact and returning it as the body rebounds.

Flapping flight generates both lift and thrust from the motion of the wings. On the downstroke the wing pushes air downward and backward, and the wing changes its angle and shape through the cycle to keep producing useful force on the upstroke. The high power demand of flight is met by enlarged flight muscles and, in birds, by an efficient unidirectional respiratory system.

Fish swim by passing waves of muscular contraction down the body, pushing against the surrounding water. Streamlined fast swimmers such as tuna concentrate the motion in the tail and confine the body to small oscillations, minimising drag. Slower or more manoeuvrable fish undulate more of the body or rely on fin movements, trading speed for precise control.

Snakes move without limbs using several distinct gaits. In lateral undulation the body pushes sideways against irregularities in the ground, in rectilinear motion the belly scales are drawn forward and planted in waves, and in sidewinding the snake throws loops of its body forward, leaving disconnected tracks. Each gait suits a different substrate, from open desert sand to confined burrows.

The cost of moving a given distance scales with body size in a regular way. Larger animals expend less energy per unit of body mass to travel a metre than smaller ones, so the mass-specific cost of transport declines with size. Among the modes of locomotion, swimming is the cheapest, flying is intermediate, and running on land is the most expensive per unit distance.

Many animals exploit elastic structures to enhance their movement. Kangaroos store and return energy in the tendons of their hind legs as they hop, so that at moderate speeds hopping costs little more than standing still. Insects such as fleas and locusts load elastic protein in advance and release it suddenly to power jumps far beyond the reach of muscle contraction alone.

Terrestrial animals change gait as they speed up, switching from a walk to a trot and then to a gallop. The transitions are not arbitrary; each gait has a range of speeds where it is most economical, and animals tend to switch at the speed where the next gait becomes cheaper. The pattern suggests that minimising the energetic cost of movement shapes the choice of gait.

Gliding is a low-cost form of aerial locomotion used by animals that cannot truly fly. Flying squirrels, certain frogs, and some lizards extend membranes or webbed feet to increase their surface area, slowing their descent and converting height into horizontal distance. Gliding lets these animals travel between trees and escape predators without the high power demand of flapping flight.

Very small organisms swim in a world dominated by viscosity rather than inertia. Because a bacterium that stops beating its flagellum halts almost instantly, the reciprocal back-and-forth motions that propel larger swimmers are useless at this scale. Bacteria instead rotate helical flagella like corkscrews, a non-reciprocal motion that generates net thrust even in the absence of inertia.

Some marine animals propel themselves by jet propulsion. A squid draws water into its mantle cavity and then contracts the muscular wall sharply, expelling the water through a narrow funnel and driving itself in the opposite direction. The funnel can be aimed to steer, and the squid alternates gentle fin swimming for cruising with rapid jetting for sudden escape.

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron, a long tubule that processes blood filtrate into urine. Each nephron begins at a glomerulus, where a tuft of capillaries filters plasma into the surrounding capsule. The filtrate then passes through successive tubule segments that reclaim useful substances and secrete wastes, fine-tuning the composition before it leaves the body.

The proximal tubule reclaims the bulk of the filtered load. It reabsorbs essentially all of the filtered glucose and amino acids, the majority of the sodium, bicarbonate, and water, and much of the filtered potassium. Because these reabsorptive processes have a finite capacity, glucose appears in the urine when the filtered amount exceeds what the transporters can recover.

The loop of Henle establishes the osmotic gradient that makes concentrated urine possible. Its descending limb is permeable to water but not salt, and its ascending limb actively pumps salt out but is impermeable to water. This countercurrent multiplier builds a steep gradient in the medulla, with the deepest tissue several times more concentrated than blood plasma.

The final concentration of the urine is set in the collecting duct under hormonal control. The hormone vasopressin, released when the body is dehydrated, makes the duct permeable to water by inserting aquaporin channels into the cell membrane. Water then flows out of the duct into the concentrated medulla, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced, conserving body water.

The kidney does more than excrete waste; it regulates the acid-base balance of the blood. It reclaims filtered bicarbonate and generates new bicarbonate by secreting hydrogen ions into the tubule, where they are buffered by phosphate and ammonia. By adjusting the rate of acid secretion, the kidney compensates for the metabolic production of acid and helps hold blood pH within a narrow range.

Beyond filtration, the kidney functions as an endocrine organ. It secretes the hormone erythropoietin in response to low oxygen, stimulating the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells. It releases renin to regulate blood pressure, and it carries out the final activation step of vitamin D, converting it to the form that promotes calcium absorption in the gut.

Osmoregulation maintains the concentration of body fluids despite variable intake and loss of water and salt. Specialised osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood concentration and trigger both the sensation of thirst and the release of vasopressin. The two responses, one behavioural and one physiological, work together to defend a stable internal osmotic environment.

Freshwater invertebrates face a constant osmotic influx of water and must work to retain salts. Many possess specialised organs, such as the contractile vacuoles of protists or the antennal glands of crustaceans, that bail out excess water. They also actively absorb ions from the dilute surrounding water across their body surfaces, expending energy to hold their internal salt concentration above that of their habitat.

Marine birds and reptiles that drink seawater rely on salt glands to rid themselves of the excess salt. Located near the eyes or nostrils, these glands secrete a fluid far more concentrated in salt than the animal's urine could achieve. The kidney alone cannot produce urine concentrated enough to excrete the salt load, so the salt gland provides the extra excretory capacity.

The volume and concentration of blood are regulated together through interacting hormonal systems. When blood volume falls, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system promotes retention of sodium and therefore water. When the heart's atria are stretched by excess volume, they release a natriuretic peptide that promotes the excretion of sodium, providing a counterbalancing signal that lowers blood volume.

Hosts and their parasites are locked in a reciprocal evolutionary struggle. A parasite that overcomes a host defence spreads, which selects for hosts carrying a new resistance, which in turn selects for parasites that can counter it. This continuous arms race drives rapid evolution in the genes of both partners, particularly those encoding the molecules of attack and defence.

The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that sexual reproduction persists because it lets hosts stay ahead of their parasites. By reshuffling resistance genes every generation, sex produces offspring with novel combinations that parasites adapted to the parental genotypes cannot exploit. Populations under heavy parasite pressure are observed to favour sexual over asexual reproduction, supporting the idea.

Negative frequency-dependent selection maintains genetic diversity in host-parasite systems. Parasites adapt to whatever host genotype is currently common, which lowers that genotype's fitness and lets rarer genotypes increase. As a rare type becomes common it is in turn targeted, so the system cycles, and no single resistance allele can sweep to fixation.

The virulence of a parasite is itself an evolved trait shaped by transmission. A parasite that exploits its host too aggressively may kill it before spreading, while one that is too gentle is outcompeted. The level of virulence that evolves often reflects a trade-off, with the optimum depending on how the parasite is transmitted and how many hosts it can reach.

Many plants resist pathogens through gene-for-gene recognition. A plant resistance gene encodes a receptor that detects the product of a corresponding pathogen avirulence gene, triggering a defensive response. The pathogen can escape detection by losing or altering that gene, which in turn selects the plant population for receptors that recognise the changed pathogen, perpetuating the coevolutionary cycle.

Parasites frequently manipulate host behaviour to complete their life cycles. The lancet liver fluke alters the behaviour of an infected ant, driving it to climb to the tip of a grass blade and clamp on, where it is likely to be eaten by the grazing mammal in which the fluke must reproduce. Such manipulation is an extended phenotype of the parasite's genes.

Coevolution proceeds at different rates and outcomes across a species' geographic range, producing a geographic mosaic. In some populations a host and parasite are tightly matched, in others one partner is locally absent, and gene flow mixes the local adaptations. The shifting mosaic of hotspots and coldspots keeps the interaction dynamic and prevents any single outcome from spreading everywhere.

Brood parasites such as the cuckoo lay their eggs in the nests of other birds, exploiting the parental care of the host. Hosts evolve the ability to recognise and reject foreign eggs, and cuckoos respond by evolving eggs that closely mimic the host's own in colour and pattern. Distinct cuckoo lineages specialise on different hosts, each with its own matched egg type.

Coevolution does not always escalate into conflict; it can soften into mutualism. A parasite that is reliably transmitted alongside its host may evolve reduced virulence and even provide a benefit, converting exploitation into cooperation. Some inherited bacterial symbionts of insects, descended from parasitic ancestors, now supply nutrients essential to the host's survival.

The immune systems of vertebrates carry signatures of their long history with parasites. The genes of the major histocompatibility complex, which present pathogen fragments to the immune system, are among the most variable in the genome. Parasite-driven selection favours rare and diverse variants, and this balancing selection preserves an exceptional pool of alleles across the population.

Bird flight muscles are among the most metabolically active tissues known. The pectoralis powers the downstroke and the smaller supracoracoideus pulls the wing back up through a tendon that runs over the shoulder like a pulley. These muscles are dense with mitochondria and capillaries to sustain the high rate of aerobic energy production that continuous flapping demands.

Insect flight muscles fall into two functional classes. Synchronous muscles contract once for each nerve impulse, suiting slower wingbeats. Asynchronous muscles, found in flies and bees, contract many times per nerve impulse because they are activated by being stretched, which lets the wings beat at frequencies far higher than the nervous system could individually command.

Hovering is the most energetically demanding form of flight because the animal must generate all its lift without the help of forward airspeed. Hummingbirds achieve it by producing lift on both the forward and backward strokes of the wing, rotating the wing at each reversal. Their flight muscles, heart, and metabolic rate are all extreme adaptations to the cost of staying still in the air.

Insect wings generate more lift than steady aerodynamics predicts because of unsteady flow effects. As the wing sweeps, a leading-edge vortex forms and clings to its upper surface, lowering the pressure there and boosting lift. Further force is recovered when the wing rotates at the end of a stroke and when it interacts with the wake left by the previous stroke.

Birds fuel long migrations primarily by burning fat, which yields far more energy per unit mass than carbohydrate. Before departure a migrant bird gorges and may nearly double its body mass with fat, while reversibly enlarging its flight muscles and shrinking its digestive organs. The shed organ mass and stored fuel together optimise the bird for the demands of sustained flight.

Soaring birds extract energy from the atmosphere rather than from their own muscles. They circle within rising columns of warm air called thermals to gain height, then glide between thermals, losing altitude slowly. Albatrosses instead exploit the gradient of wind speed above the ocean surface, repeatedly turning into and away from the wind in a manoeuvre called dynamic soaring.

The high oxygen demand of flight is met by respiratory systems of unusual efficiency. Birds pass air through their lungs in one direction with the help of air sacs, maintaining a steady oxygen gradient. Insects deliver oxygen directly to their flight muscles through fine tracheal tubes, and rhythmic compression of the tubes during flight actively ventilates the tissue.

Many flying insects must warm their flight muscles before they can take off. Bumblebees and moths shiver, contracting opposing muscle groups against one another to generate heat without moving the wings. Only once the thoracic temperature reaches a working threshold can the muscles contract fast and forcefully enough to sustain flight, which is why a cold bee may sit and vibrate before departing.

Flying animals control their movement with continuous sensory feedback. Insects carry tiny club-shaped organs called halteres, modified hindwings that vibrate and act as gyroscopes, sensing rotation of the body and allowing rapid corrective steering. Birds rely on vision, the vestibular system, and arrays of sensors in the wing feathers to monitor airflow and adjust their wing surfaces in flight.

The feather is the structure that makes bird flight possible. A flight feather has a central shaft from which barbs branch, and the barbs carry interlocking barbules with tiny hooks that zip the surface into a continuous, lightweight, and slightly flexible vane. The arrangement creates an airfoil strong enough to bear aerodynamic load yet able to be repaired by simple preening.

Receptor tyrosine kinases convert the binding of a growth factor into an intracellular signal. The ligand brings two receptors together, and the paired receptors phosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. These phosphorylated sites become docking points that recruit signalling proteins, assembling a complex at the membrane that launches the downstream cascade.

The mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade amplifies and relays growth signals through three tiers of kinases that successively phosphorylate one another. Because each kinase activates many copies of the next, a small input is greatly amplified, and the multiple steps allow regulation and the integration of additional inputs. The final kinase enters the nucleus and switches on genes that drive proliferation.

Second messengers spread a signal rapidly through the cytoplasm. The hydrolysis of a membrane lipid releases inositol trisphosphate, which diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens channels that release stored calcium. The resulting rise in cytosolic calcium acts as a near-universal signal, controlling processes as varied as secretion, contraction, and gene expression.

Many signalling pathways act through reversible protein phosphorylation. A kinase adds a phosphate group to a target protein and a phosphatase removes it, and the balance of the two enzyme activities sets the fraction of the target that is modified. Because phosphorylation can change a protein's shape, activity, or binding partners, this switch is one of the most widespread mechanisms of cellular control.

The small GTPase Ras acts as a molecular switch in growth-factor signalling. It is active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP, and accessory proteins control the switch by promoting either nucleotide exchange or GTP hydrolysis. Mutations that lock Ras in the active state drive uncontrolled proliferation and are among the most common genetic lesions in human cancer.

Cell signalling pathways often determine survival or death. Survival signals activate kinases that keep pro-apoptotic proteins in check, while withdrawal of those signals tips the balance toward apoptosis. The death receptor pathway works in the opposite direction, with an extracellular death ligand directly recruiting and activating the caspases that dismantle the cell.

Notch signalling allows a cell to influence the fate of the cell it directly touches. The Notch receptor on one cell binds a ligand on the neighbouring cell, and the pulling force triggers cleavage of the receptor. The released intracellular fragment travels to the nucleus and joins a transcription complex, converting a contact between two cells into a change in gene expression.

Signalling pathways are not isolated lines but a connected network with extensive crosstalk. One pathway can amplify or dampen another, and many converge on shared targets. This interconnection lets a cell integrate the multiple signals it receives at once, so that the response to any one cue depends on the full context of the others arriving at the same time.

Signalling responses are shaped not only by which pathway is active but by the dynamics of the signal. A brief pulse of activity in a pathway can drive a cell to proliferate while sustained activity of the same pathway drives it to differentiate. Cells therefore read the duration, amplitude, and frequency of a signal, extracting information from its temporal pattern.

Termination is as important as activation in cell signalling. Once a signal has been received, the cell must reset so it can respond again. Receptors are internalised and degraded or recycled, activating enzymes are switched off, and second messengers are rapidly broken down. Without these shut-off mechanisms a cell would remain locked in its response and lose the ability to sense new information.
